The Moxeño is a traditional wind instrument from eastern Bolivia in the Amazon basin of South America, created by the indigenous Moxeño people and several hundred years old. It is made of a bamboo tube and is plain and unadorned in appearance. Its timbre is warm and slightly nasal, between the brightness of a flute and the fullness of a reed pipe; its range lies in the upper middle register, and the timbre is bright yet steady, with good carrying power. The instrument can produce natural, harmonious overtones that give the sound a sense of layering. The Moxeño blends Spanish and African musical elements to form a distinctive Latin American style, particularly suited to expressing regional character and plainness.
莫克塞尼管是玻利維亞莫克塞尼民族的傳統管樂器，音色具有溫暖而略帶鼻音的特質，介於: The Moxeño is a traditional wind instrument of the Moxeño people of Bolivia, with a warm timbre that is slightly nasal, between the brightness of a flute and the fullness of a reed pipe. Its range is usually in the upper middle register, and its timbre is on the bright side without losing steadiness, with some carrying power. Its resonance depends on the unusual construction of the tube and can produce natural, harmonious overtones, giving the sound a sense of layering. Compared with other traditional wind instruments of South America, the Moxeño's timbre is warmer and more human, not as deep and distant as the clay ocarina, but with a rounder quality than the bamboo flute. Its timbre combines regional character with plainness, and suits in particular the bleakness and depth of the Andean highlands.

This traditional instrument was created by the local indigenous Moxeño people and is several hundred years old. It is made of a bamboo tube and produces its distinctive timbre through a simple and ingenious design.

Since the twentieth century, with the growth of ethnomusicology and of cultural preservation movements, the instrument has come to be valued and promoted. Today's world-music listeners have spread it worldwide through field recordings and ethnomusicological research. It now keeps its traditional uses in the Amazon region and is also an important instrument in international folk-music performance and academic study.
